newsitem.title: UK: Markka move to intensify lira ERM fever--analysts.
newsitem.headline: Markka move to intensify lira ERM fever--analysts.

text.p: Finland's decision to link the markka to the European exchange rate mechanism came as no big surprise to financial markets but it is bound to intensify speculation that another ERM pretender, the lira, will go in soon, financial analysts said on Sunday.
Both currencies are likely to rally in a knee-jerk reaction to the move even though the markka's 3.04 per mark central rate was bang in line with market expectations.

"This is not a surprise and confirms the positive political sentiment in favour of European monetary union (EMU) throughout Europe and will now focus attention on when the lira will enter the system," said Gerard Lyons, chief economist at DKB International in London.
The markka was trading at around 2.9870 per mark in late European trading on Friday, having firmed by around six percent since late April.

The markka has joined with 15 percent fluctuation bands, which is the case for all members except the mark and Dutch guilder which maintained a 2.25 percent range when the ERM was reshaped on August 1, 1993.

But member countries have been trying hard to shadow their old 2.25 percent limits and it is suspected the Finns will do the same, but analysts said they may have to let the markka trade out to perhaps five percent either side of the central rate.

"The knee-jerk will be that the markka will tend to strengthen," said Stephen King, international economist at HSBC Markets. "Locking yourself into an institution in a public way suggests you are even more committed to maintaining your currency so there is less downside risk."
Between now and the end of the year speculation of lira entry will keep the currency firm but the case is less clear cut and the market is more unsure about the likely central rate.

The lira's central rate will be a sticking point, with France already pushing for a firmer lira but Italian industry beginning to complain about its recent rise and warning the government not to peg it at too high a level.
"The French and the Germans want the lira to be at a strong level when it enters the ERM, say around 950 (per mark) but the Italians would be happier above 1,000," DKB's Lyons said.

Analysts said that, as the Italian budget will probably not be finalised in parliament until closer to the end of the year, a good time to put the lira in would be around the time of the Dublin EU summit of heads of state and government in early December.

"It would be an obvious time to do it and if they can agree an appropriate central rate (German Chancellor Helmut) Kohl and (French President Jacques) Chirac would love it if the Italians went back in because it would give the whole EMU process more support," HSBC's King said.
The Finnish move also has positive implications for sterling, analysts said.

Sterling is being dragged up in line with EMU convergence trades, but is seen being a safe-haven from any European turmoil that might result if the EMU process begins to crumble. Most traders do not believe that Britain will be in the first EMU group in 1999.
